1.21.m: Pulastya said: / Formerly, in the Bṛhat-kalpa, there was a lord of men who was the embodiment of dharma, / a friend of Śakra, by whom thousands of daityas had been slain,
by whose radiance the moon, the sun, and the rest became bereft of luster, / and by whom hundreds of dānavas were defeated;
who could assume any form at will, and though human, was undefeated. / His chaste wife was Bhānumatī, the beauty of the three worlds,
who in beauty like Lakṣmī surpassed the beauties of the immortals; / she was that king's chief queen, dearer to him even than life.
She shone like Śrī in the midst of ten thousand women; / by a thousand crores of kings she could never be equaled.
Once, seated in his assembly hall, filled with wonder, / having bowed to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, he asked his family priest:
‘Reverend Sir, by what merit is my fortune unexcelled, / and why is there immense, ever-surpassing splendor in my body?’
Vasiṣṭha said: / ‘Formerly, there was a courtesan named Līlāvatī, devoted to Śiva; / by her, a mountain of salt was given at Puṣkara on the fourteenth lunar day,
together with golden trees and immortals, properly according to rule. / A Śūdra who was a goldsmith became the artisan then.
[As] a servant in Līlāvatī's house, golden trees with golden flowers / were fashioned by him, full of faith, O king.
Endowed with exquisite form, they were beautifully made. / Knowing it was a sacred duty, he took no wages.
And the trees made of gold were polished by his wife. / And in Līlāvatī's house, O king, service was performed,
Such as attending upon Brahmins, rendered by both of them without deceit. / And in the course of time, O sinless one, that courtesan Līlāvatī,
Freed from all sins, went to the abode of Śiva. / And that goldsmith who was poor, yet of great fortitude,
Took no payment from the courtesan; he is you in this present world: / you have become the lord of the seven continents, radiant as ten thousand suns.
And the wife by whom the goldsmith's golden trees were thoroughly polished, / she is this Bhānumatī of yours.

Therefore you are unconquered among men, and [your] fortune is endowed with health and good luck; / therefore, O king, you too should duly present the mountain of grain and the others according to rule.

Pulastya said: / Saying "So be it," that embodiment of true righteousness honoured Vasiṣṭha's word and gave / all the mountains of grain and the others according to rule; honoured by the gods, he went to the world of the Enemy of Smara.
If one sees these being brought forward, touches them being given here by men, / listens with devotion, or sets his mind on them, he too, purified of sin, goes to heaven.

A man attains the quelling of bad dreams through the reading about these kingly mountains that shatter fear of worldly existence; / what need be said, O bull among kings, of one who, with a calm mind, properly makes a gift of all the lordly mountains?

Bhīṣma said: / Is there any fasting or vow capable of extinguishing the fire of grief caused by separation from what is cherished, / bringing permanent prosperity on this earth, and destroying a man's fear of worldly existence?

Pulastya said: / This that you have asked is dear to the world, difficult even for the wise to obtain because of its greatness; / yet to you, who are devoted, I will declare the vow hidden among gods, asuras, and mortals.
In the month of Āśvayuja is the meritorious vow of Viśokadvādaśī. / Eating lightly on the tenth day, the wise man should begin it with restraint;
Facing north or facing east, preceded by cleaning the teeth, / abstaining from food on the eleventh, having duly worshipped Keśava
And having worshipped Śrī according to rule, [resolving:] "I will eat on the next day." / Having made this resolve, sleeping, and rising at dawn, the person
Should bathe with all medicinal herbs and water mixed with the five products of the cow; / wearing white garlands and clothes, he should worship the Lord of Śrī with blue lotuses:
"Homage to Viśoka!" the two feet; and the shanks indeed "To the Granter of Boons!"; / the knees likewise "To the Lord of Śrī!"; and the thighs "To the One who sleeps on the water!";
"Homage to Kandarpa!" the secret parts; "Homage to Mādhava!" the hips; / "To Dāmodara!" the belly; and the flanks indeed "To the Vast One!";
The navel "To the Lotus-naveled One!"; the heart indeed "To Manmatha!"; / the chest of the Lord "To Śrīdhara!"; the two hands "Homage to the Slayer of Madhu!";
"Homage to Vaikuṇṭha!" the neck; the face indeed "To the Lotus-faced One!"; / the nose "To the Treasure of Freedom from Grief!"; and the eyes "To Vāsudeva!";
The forehead "To Vāmana!"; and again the eyebrows "To Hari!"; / the hair "To Mādhava!"; the diadem "To the Universal-formed One!";
Likewise the head "Homage to the Self of All!": thus he should worship. / Having thus worshipped Govinda with incenses, garlands, and ointments,
Then, having drawn a mandala, he should prepare an altar of earth, / square on all sides, one cubit in measure, sloping to the north,
Smooth and pleasing, surrounded all around with three ramparts; / the ramparts are three finger-breadths in height, and their width two finger-breadths.
Above the altar, the wall should be eight finger-breadths high. / With river sand he should make a sun, [and] place an image of Lakṣmī upon it.
On the altar, the wise man should worship Lakṣmī seated in the middle of the sun: / "Homage to the Goddess! Homage to Peace! Homage to Lakṣmī! Homage to Śrī!
Homage to Contentment! Homage to Nourishment! Homage to Creation! Homage to Sight! Homage! Homage! / Viśokā, for the destruction of sorrow! Viśokā, granter of boons, homage to you!
May Viśokā be for my prosperity! Viśokā, for the attainment of all success!" / Then, having wrapped the sun in white garments, he should worship it with fruits,
Likewise with various kinds of foods and with a golden lotus. / And in silver vessels the wise man should place water with darbha grass.
Then he should have dancing and singing performed for the whole night. / When three watches have passed, the person, rising then,
Should approach and worship couples of Brahmins, / three or one according to ability, with clothes, garlands, and ointments;
[These couples] resting upon beds are to be worshipped with: "Homage to the One who sleeps on the water!" / Then, after keeping vigil during the night with singing and instrumental music,
In the morning, having bathed, he should worship the married couple; / and he should feed them according to his ability, free from deceit regarding wealth.
Having listened to the Purāṇas with devotion, he should pass that day. / By this rule he should perform everything month after month.
At the end of the vow he should give a bed accompanied by a molasses-cow, / with pillows and footrests, equipped with fine coverlets and draperies:
"Just as Lakṣmī does not abandon you, O Lord of Men, and depart, / so may beauty, health, and freedom from grief always be mine;
Just as Lakṣmī never exists separated from the God, / so may freedom from grief be mine, and foremost devotion to Keśava!"
With this mantra, the bed accompanied by a molasses-cow, / and the sun together with Lakṣmī, should be given by one desiring prosperity.
Blue lotus, or oleander, amaranth and saffron, / screw-pine, chaste tree, jasmine, fragrant trumpet-flower,
Kadamba, wild rose, and Spanish jasmine—these are always commended. / Bhīṣma said: / Declare also the procedure of the molasses-cow, O best of sages!
Of what form, and with what mantra should it be given? Let that be spoken here. / Pulastya said: / The form and the fruit of the molasses-cow procedure here,
That, which destroys all sins, I will now proclaim: / One should spread a black antelope skin of four cubits on the ground, with its neck facing east,
On ground smeared with cow dung, scattering darbha grass all around; / likewise one should fashion a calf from a small antelope skin.
One should fashion the cow facing east, or make a cow with her calf out of clay. / An excellent molasses-cow would always consist of four bhāras;
One should make the calf with one bhāra; a middling one is prescribed as two bhāras, / with the calf being half a bhāra; but the lowest is made with one bhāra,
And the calf with a fourth part, according to the wealth of the house. / Both the cow and calf made should be covered with fine white cloth,
Having pearl-oyster ears, sugarcane legs, pure pearl eyes, / white thread veins, white blanket dewlaps,
Two copper plates for backs, white fly-whisk tails, / coral eyebrows, provided with butter udders,
Furnished with gold eyes, sapphire pupils, / silk tails, bronze milking vessels, white and very lovely,
With golden horn-ornaments and feet rich in silver, / furnished with diverse fruits, with scent-boxes for nostrils.
Having arranged [it] in this way, one should worship with incense and lamps: / "She who is the Lakṣmī of all beings, and she who resides in the gods,

May that goddess, in the form of a cow, who is the Fortune of all living beings and who dwells in the gods, remove my sin! / She who is the Fortune on the chest of Viṣṇu, and she who is Svāhā in fire,
and she who is the power of the moon, the sun, and Śakra—may that cow grant me boons! / Since you are Svadhā of the chief ancestors, and Svāhā of the eaters of sacrifice,
and the cow that removes all sins, therefore grant me prosperity! / Having thus addressed that cow, one should present it to a brāhmaṇa.
This procedure is recited for all cows. / The ten cows which destroy sin are recited:
I shall state their nature and their names, O lord of men. / The first is the molasses-cow, and next is the clarified-butter-cow;
the third is the sesame-cow, and the fourth is named the water[-cow]; / the fifth is the milk-cow, and next is the honey-cow;
the seventh is the sugar-cow, and the eighth is fashioned of curd; / the ninth is the juice-cow, and the tenth is in its own [living] form.
For the liquid cows, there should be jars; for the others, heaps of their own substances. / Moreover, some men in this context desire a gold-cow,
and other great sages [prescribe one] made of fresh butter and of oils. / The procedure is the very same, and the traditional furnishings are the same.
Combined with mantras and invocations, they should always be given at every sacred junction, / just like a śrāddha, granting the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
In connection with the molasses-cow, all of them have been declared to you by me; / they grant the fruit of all sacrifices, remove all sins, and are auspicious.
Because the Viśokadvādaśī vow is the best of vows, / the molasses-cow is praised here precisely as an ancillary to it.
At a solstice, at an equinox, on an auspicious vyatīpāta, and further / on sacred days such as eclipses, the molasses-cow and the others should be given.
And this Viśokadvādaśī is auspicious, removing all sins; / fasting on it, a man goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
In this world he gains good fortune, long life, and health; / he reaches the city of Viṣṇu, and at death he remembers Hari.
For ninety-eight thousand cosmic ages, O king who knows dharma, / no grief, suffering, or misfortune befalls him.
Or a woman who performs this Viśokadvādaśī, / constantly devoted to dance and song, she also obtains that fruit.

Because dance, song, and music before Hari are endless; / whoever reads this thus, whoever hears it properly here, / or whoever watches the worship of the enemy of Madhu, Mura, and Naraka,

And he who gives thought to the people, in Indra's world / he dwells, worshipped by the hosts of gods for one kalpa.
Bhīṣma said: / O Lord, I wish to hear the supreme glorification of the gifts
which is imperishable in the other world and revered by hosts of divine sages. / Pulastya said: / I shall describe the gift of Meru in ten ways, O best of kings,
by bestowing which the giver attains endless worlds revered by the gods. / Not in the Purāṇas, nor in the Vedas, nor in sacrifices, nor in temples
is that fruit obtained which one enjoys here when they are studied or performed; / therefore I shall describe the gift of the mountains in due order.
The first is the grain-mountain, and the second is the salt-mountain; / the third is the molasses-mountain, and the fourth is the gold-mountain;
the fifth is the sesame-mountain, and the sixth is the cotton-mountain; / the seventh is the clarified-butter-mountain, and the eighth is the jewel-mountain;
likewise the ninth is of silver, and the tenth is the sugar-mountain. / I will explain the procedure for these in proper order.
At a solstice, or on an auspicious vyatīpāta, on a day-loss, / on the third tithi of the bright fortnight, during an eclipse, or on the new moon,
during weddings, festivals, or sacrifices, or on the twelfth tithi, / or on the bright fifteenth tithi, or under an auspicious lunar mansion according to rule,
the grain-mountain and the others should be given on the full moon of Kārttika at Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara, / or at holy bathing places, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or in the courtyard of a house.
One should faithfully construct a square pavilion facing north, / sloping toward the northeast, auspicious, or facing east according to rule.
On the ground smeared with cow dung, having spread kuśa grass, / in its center one should make the mountain, accompanied by the supporting mountains.
With a thousand droṇas of grain, the mountain here is the best; / the intermediate is with five hundred, and the lowest is with three hundred.
Meru in the center should be made of abundant rice, endowed with three golden trees; / its summit and its garments should be fashioned in manifold ways by the best of twice-borns.
There should be four silver peaks, and the slope regions should also be of silver; / on the east it should be furnished with pearls and diamonds, on the south with hessonite and rubies,
on the west with emeralds and sapphires, on the north with cat's eyes and topazes; / surrounded by pieces of sandalwood and corals, furnished with creepers, and rich in pearl stones.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Lord who is the foe of Pura, and the sun should also be made of gold here; / likewise its caves should be covered with sugarcane stalks, and it should have streams of clarified butter and water flowing in the directions.
White cloths should form the series of clouds on the east, yellow ones on the south, / variegated garments on the west, and dense red ones on the north.
Having duly installed the eight world-guardians headed by Mahendra, made of silver, / there should be a variety of groves all around, along with charming garlands and ointments,
and above, a five-colored canopy decorated with unfading white flowers. / Having thus arranged the foremost immortal mountain, one should next place the supporting mountains of Meru
in a fourth of its size in the four directions, rich in flowers and unguents: / on the east, Mandara, endowed with many fruits and shining with a golden Kāma;
on the south, Gandhamādana is to be set up, made of a heap of wheat and of silver, / equipped with a golden lord of sacrifice, a lake of clarified butter, cloth, and groves of silver;

on the west, one should construct the sesame-mountain, with many fragrant flowers, a golden pippala tree, and a golden swan, / likewise with a silver flower grove, accompanied by cloth, and with the lake Sitoda of curds in front of it;

having placed that Vipula mountain, then on the north one should construct the Supārśva mountain made of black gram, along with cloth / and flowers, crowned by a golden banyan tree and shining with a golden banner,

with a honey lake, the Bhadrasaras, and with a silver grove likewise, having furnished it with a radiant canopy. / Then an oblational offering is to be made by four foremost twice-borns, experts in the Vedas and Purāṇas, self-restrained and of blameless conduct and form.

Having fashioned a pit of one cubit's measure on the east, the offering is to be made with sesame, barley, clarified butter, kindling, and kuśa grass; / and at night a vigil is to be kept with gentle forms of singing. And I will declare the invocation of the mountains:

‘O immortal mountain, abode and treasury of all the hosts of gods, quickly destroy what is adverse in our houses! / Bestow safety and bring about supreme peace; worshipped by me with supreme devotion, come!’
‘You indeed are the Lord, the Ruler, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun; / you are the seed consisting of the formed and the unformed. Therefore protect me, O eternal one!’
‘Since you are the dwelling of the world-guardians, of him whose form is the universe, / and of the Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus, therefore grant me peace!’
"Since your head is never devoid of gods and women, / therefore deliver me from this miserable ocean of saṃsāra."
Having thus worshipped that Meru, he should also venerate Mandara: / "Since with the Caitraratha grove and with Bhadrāśva, O mountain,
you shine, O Mandara, quickly bring me joy therefore. / Since you are the crest-jewel in Jambūdvīpa, O Gandhamādana,
possessing the radiance of the hosts of Gandharvas, may my fame be steadfast from this. / Since you, with Ketumāla and the Vaibhrāja forest,
possess the lustre of golden rocks, may my prosperity be permanent from this. / Since with the Northern Kurus and with the Sāvitra forest,
O king Supārśva, you are ever glorious, may my fortune be imperishable from this." / Having thus invoked them all, again, at clear daybreak,
having bathed, he should give the central, best of mountains to the guru; / and, O king, he should give the buttress-mountains in order to the officiating priests.
Twenty-four cows should be given, or else ten, O ruler of the earth; / or according to ability, seven or eight, or an incapable man may give five.

Even a single brown or milch cow should be given to the guru. / This very rite is declared for all the mountains;

the very same mantras are remembered in the worship, and the very same accessories, / for the planets, the guardians of the world, and Brahmā and the others everywhere.
The oblation is recited with their own respective mantras in all the mountains. / One should always observe a fast; if unable, an evening meal is approved.
Hear, O king, the procedure for all the mountains in order, / as well as the mantras used in the gifts, according to their reward.
"Since food is declared to be Brahman, and food is celebrated as the vital breaths, / [and] from food beings arise, and the world thrives by food;
since food alone is Lakṣmī, and food alone is Janārdana— / therefore, in the form of a mountain of grain, protect [me], O best of mountains."
He who, by this procedure, gives a mountain made of grain, / is magnified in the realm of the gods for a full hundred Manvantaras.
Radiant in an aerial car crowded with hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas, / he arrives at the surface of heaven, O best of kings.
When his merits are exhausted, he attains kingship of kings in this world, without a doubt. / Now next I shall fully declare the supreme mountain of salt,
by giving which a man reaches the world together with Śiva. / The highest mountain of salt should be made with sixteen droṇas;
the intermediate with half of that; and with four, it is remembered as inferior. / A man lacking wealth may, according to his ability, have it made above a droṇa.
He should have the buttress-mountains made separately with a fourth part. / He should always perform the procedure as before for Brahmā and the others;
likewise, the entire dwelling of the world-guardians is made of gold. / Lakes, forest trees, and the like, as well as the other [details], he should arrange in the same way.
He should perform a vigil here too. Learn the mantras for the giving: / "Since this relish in salt is endowed with the essence of good fortune,
and by possessing that nature, protect me in my distress, O best of mountains. / Since all other relishes are not prominent without salt,
and you are ever dear to Śiva and Śivā, therefore be the bestower of peace! / Since, born from the body of Viṣṇu, you increase health,
therefore, in the form of a mountain, protect [me] from the ocean of saṃsāra." / He who, by this procedure, gives a mountain of salt,
dwells in the realm of Umā for an eon, and then goes to the supreme state. / Beyond this, I shall declare the excellent mountain of molasses,
by giving which a man attains heaven, venerated by the gods. / The highest is considered ten bhāras, the intermediate five;
the lowest should be three bhāras; a man of little wealth [may give] with half of that. / In the same way the invocation, worship, golden trees, worship of the gods,
the buttress-mountains likewise, lakes, forest deities, / oblation, night vigil, and the consecration of the world-guardians,
he should perform like the mountain of grain, and utter this mantra: / "Just as among the gods this Janārdana, the soul of all, is supreme;
just as the Sāmaveda is among the Vedas, Mahādeva among yogins, / the Praṇava among all mantras, and Pārvatī among women;
so sugarcane juice is always considered supreme among juices: / may the mountain of molasses therefore grant me supreme fortune.
Since, O mountain of molasses, you are the abode of the giver of good fortune / and you were fashioned by Pārvatī, therefore protect me always."
He who, by this procedure, gives a mountain made of molasses, / being worshipped by Gandharvas, is magnified in the realm of Gaurī.
And at the end of a hundred eons he becomes sovereign of the seven continents, / endowed with long life and health, and undefeated by enemies.
Next, I shall declare the supreme mountain of gold that removes sin, / through the giving of which men go to the abode of Viriñci.
The highest is a thousand palas, the intermediate five hundred; / with half of that is the lowest; likewise, even a man of little wealth,
free from malice, should give above one pala according to his ability. / He should arrange everything like the mountain of grain, O best of kings,
and in the same way he should present the buttress-mountains to the officiating priests: / "Homage to you, the seed of all, having Brahman within your womb, homage!
Since you bestow endless fruits, therefore protect [me], O mass of rocks! / Since you are the child of Agni, since you are the son of the Lord of the World,
therefore, in the form of a mountain of gold, protect [me], O best of mountains!" / He who, by this procedure, gives a mountain of gold,
goes to the supreme world of Brahmā, which brings bliss; / he remains there for a hundred eons, and then goes to the supreme state.
Now next I shall fully declare the mountain of sesame according to rule, / by giving which a man goes to the unexcelled world of Viṣṇu.
The mountain of sesame is celebrated as highest with ten droṇas, intermediate with five, / and lowest with three, O best of kings.
And all else, the buttress-mountains and the rest, is as before. / I shall declare the mantra for giving properly, O bull among kings:
"Since at the slaying of Madhu, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and māṣa beans / were born from the sweat of Viṣṇu's body, therefore be the bestower of peace!
And since sesame seeds are indeed the protection in offerings to the gods and ancestors, / produce prosperity, O lord of mountains; O mountain of sesame, homage to you!"
Invoking [her] in this way, he who gives an incomparable mountain of sesame / goes to the realm of Viṣṇu, from which return is hard to obtain.
And the mountain of cotton here is highest with twenty bhāras; / it is declared intermediate with ten, and considered lowest with five.
A man of little wealth, free from financial dishonesty, may give with one bhāra. / Everything should be prepared like the mountain of grain, O best of kings.
And when the night has turned to morning, he should give it, uttering this: / "Since you alone are always the covering for the worlds here,
O cotton mountain, homage! Therefore be the destroyer of the flood of sins!" / Whoever thus gives a lordly mountain of cotton in the presence of Śarva,
dwells in the world of Rudra for an eon, and then becomes a king here. / Now next I shall fully declare the unexcelled mountain of clarified butter;
Clarified butter is full of fiery energy, holy, and a destroyer of great sins. / The best mountain of clarified butter is made with twenty jars of clarified butter;
The middling is said to be of ten, and the lowest is considered to be of five. / Even a person of little wealth may make it here with two, according to rule.
Likewise, one should prepare the supporting mountains with a quarter [of the material]. / One should place vessels of unbroken rice above the jars.
One should cause them to be compact and tall, suitably handsome according to rule. / One should wrap them with white garments, sugarcane stalks, fruits, and the like.

The entire procedure here is recited to be like that for the grain mountain, / preceded indeed by the preliminary consecration; similarly, the oblation into fire and worship of the gods [are the same].
And when the night has turned to dawn, with a calm mind, / one should present [it] to the guru, and likewise the supporting mountains to the officiating priests.
‘Because clarified butter arose from contact with immortal radiance, / therefore, may Śaṅkara, whose flame is clarified butter and who is the soul of the universe, be pleased here!’
‘Because Brahman, full of fiery energy, is established in clarified butter itself, / therefore, O mountain, in the form of a mountain of clarified butter, protect us!’
One who gives the supreme mountain of clarified butter according to this rule, / even if joined with great sins, goes to the world of Śambhu.
Accompanied by geese and cranes, garlanded with clusters of small bells, / on a celestial chariot, surrounded by apsarases, siddhas, and vidyādharas,
he wanders together with his ancestors until the dissolution of all beings. / Now, next, I shall proclaim the supreme mountain of jewels.
The best mountain consists of a thousand pearls; / the middling is of five hundred, and the lowest is remembered to be of three hundred.
The supporting mountains all around should be of a fourth part: / on the east with diamonds and gomeda gems, on the south with sapphires;
Gandhamādana should be made by the wise endowed with topazes; / to the west, the Vipula mountain should be intermixed with cat's-eyes and corals;
one should also place rubies with gold on the north. / Here too one should arrange everything as for the grain mountain.
Likewise, having performed the invocation, one should worship the golden trees / and gods with flowers, perfumes, and the like; at dawn, there should be the dismissal.
As before, [having offered them] to the guru and the officiating priests, one should utter this mantra: / ‘Just as all the hosts of gods reside in all jewels,
and you are eternally made of jewels, therefore protect [us], O great mountain! / Since by the gift of jewels Janārdana attains satisfaction,
therefore, O mountain, by the favor of the worship and mantra, protect us!’ / One who gives a mountain made of jewels according to this rule,
goes to the world of Viṣṇu, worshipped by the lord of the immortals. / He dwells there for a full hundred kalpas, O ruler of men.
Endowed with beauty, health, and virtues, he becomes the sovereign of the seven continents. / Whatever [sin] such as killing a brāhmaṇa has been committed by him here or in the other world,
all that goes to destruction, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. / Now, next, I shall proclaim the supreme silver mountain,
by the gift of which a man goes to the world of Soma, O best of men. / The best silver mountain is made of ten thousand palas;
the middling is said to be of five [thousand], and the lowest is remembered to be of half that. / If unable, one should always make it above twenty [palas], according to one's capacity.
Likewise, one should prepare the supporting mountains with a fourth part. / As before, one should make Mandara and the others out of silver according to rule.
The wise person should likewise have the world-guardians made of gold. / Endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the sun, the slope here should be made of gold;
the rest of those mountains should be of silver, and not of gold. / And one should perform the remaining [rites] as before, such as the oblation into fire and the night-vigil.
At dawn, one should likewise give the silver mountain to the guru, / and the supporting mountains to the officiating priests, having honored them with garments and ornaments.
Holding darbha grass in his hand, free from jealousy, he should give it while reciting this mantra: / ‘Because silver is dear to the ancestors, or to the moon and Śaṅkara,
therefore, protect us from the ocean of sorrowful worldly existence!’ / A man who, having set it up in this manner, gives the best silver mountain,
attains the fruit of ten million cows. / In the world of Soma, by gandharvas, kinnaras, and hosts of apsarases
being worshipped, the wise man dwells until the dissolution of all beings. / Now, next, I shall proclaim the supreme sugar mountain,
by the gift of which Viṣṇu, the sun, and the Rudras are always pleased. / The best great mountain is made of eight bhāras of sugar;
the middling is said to be of four, and the lowest is remembered to be of two bhāras. / He who has little wealth may make it with one bhāra or with half a bhāra.
A person should make the supporting mountains with a fourth part. / Everything should be fully provided with golden garments, like the grain mountain.
On top of Meru, three golden trees should be placed: / the mandāra, the pārijāta, and the third, the wish-granting tree.
One should place these three trees on the summit of all [mountains]. / The yellow sandalwood and the saṃtāna on the eastern and western sides
should be placed on all mountains, especially on the sugar mountain. / On Mandara, Kāmadeva should always be facing west;
on the peak of Gandhamādana, the giver of wealth should face north; / on the Vipula mountain, Haṃsa, the embodiment of the Veda, should face east;
on Supārśva, there should be the golden Surabhi facing south. / Having performed everything—invocation, sacrifice, and the like—like the grain mountain,
one should then give the best central mountain to the guru, / and the four mountains to the officiating priests, and should recite these mantras:
‘This supreme sugar mountain is the essence of the nectar of good fortune; / therefore, O king of mountains, always be a bringer of joy!’
‘Those drops of nectar of the gods which fell upon the earth as they drank— / arisen from them, O sugar mountain, protect us!’
‘Moreover, sugar arose from the middle of the bow of the mind-born [Kāma]; / you are made of that, O great mountain: protect [us] from the ocean of worldly existence!’
The man who gives the sugar mountain according to this rule, / freed from all sins, goes to the abode of Brahman.
Having mounted a celestial chariot bright as the moon and sun, with his dependents / he ascends together [with them]; then, possessing the radiance of Viṣṇu, in heaven
[he stays]; then, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he becomes the ruler of the seven continents, / endowed with long life and health, for thirty thousand births.
One should feed [others] according to one's capacity for all the mountains, free from jealousy, / and oneself should eat food free from alkali and salt, with his [the guru's] permission.
One should have all the mountain's accessories delivered to the home of the brāhmaṇa. / All this gift of mountains, which is unsurpassed, has been related to you;
ask me, O king, whatever else pleases you.’ / Bhīṣma said: / ‘O venerable one, tell me of some vow that carries one across the ocean of worldly existence,
which grants heaven and health as its fruit.’ / Pulastya said: / ‘I shall proclaim the solar observance, known by name as Kalyāṇasaptamī;
likewise Viśokasaptamī; third, Phalasaptamī; / one should perform Śarkarāsaptamī, and likewise Kamalasaptamī;
Mandārasaptamī as the sixth; and the seventh, Śubhasaptamī. / All are declared to yield holy fruit, and all are worshipped by divine seers.
I shall declare the rule for these properly and in order: / When the seventh day of the bright fortnight falls on a Sunday,’
it is indeed called Kalyāṇinī and spoken of as Vijayā. / In the morning, one should perform a bath in a river with milk from a cow;
wearing white garments, facing east, one should fashion a lotus with unbroken grains of rice, / with eight petals, in the center, and likewise a circular pericarp.
With flowers, unbroken rice grains, and water, one should install the Lord of Gods in all [directions] in order: / to the east with 'To Tapana,' and then with 'To Mārtaṇḍa;'
to the south with 'To Divākara,' to the southwest with 'To Vidhātṛ,' / to the west with 'To Varuṇa,' and to the northwest with 'To Bhāskara;'
to the north with 'To Vikartana,' and on the eighth petal with 'To Deva;' / and in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end: 'Obeisance be to the Supreme Self.'
Having worshipped [the deity] with these mantras ending in salutations, / with white garments, fruits, foodstuffs, incense, garlands, and unguents,
one should worship on a bare patch of ground with devotion, using jaggery and salt. / Then, having dismissed the best of Brahmins with the vyāhṛti mantras,

one should gratify [them] with devotion according to one's capacity, with jaggery, milk, clarified butter, and other offerings; / and one should present a vessel filled with sesame seeds and gold to a Brahmin.
Having observed this vow and slept, rising at dawn, a person, / having performed bathing and silent recitation, along with the Brahmins,
having eaten milk-rice with clarified butter, should offer to a Vedic scholar / free from the cat-vow a vessel of clarified butter together with gold and a water jar,
[saying:] 'May the blessed Lord, the Supreme Self Divākara, be pleased herein.' / By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month.
Then, in the thirteenth month, one should give thirteen cows / furnished with clothes and ornaments, with gold-tipped horns, and rich in milk.
One who lacks wealth, free from malice, should give even a single [cow]. / One should not practice deceit regarding wealth, for out of delusion one falls downward.
Whoever performs the Kalyāṇasaptamī according to this procedure / is freed from all sins and is glorified in the world of the sun.
Longevity, health, and endless sovereignty are born here [for him]. / This [vow] removes all sins and is revered by all deities.
Kalyāṇasaptamī always quells all evils. / Whoever hears or even recites this Kalyāṇasaptamī,
which grants endless fruit, is freed from sins. / In the same manner, O best of kings, I shall declare the Viśokasaptamī,
fasting upon which a person never experiences sorrow here. / In the month of Māgha, having bathed with black sesame seeds on the fifth day of the bright fortnight,
having taken a meal of spiced rice and lentils after cleaning the teeth, / having undertaken the vow of fasting, living as a celibate, one should sleep at night.
Then, rising at daybreak, having performed bathing and silent recitation, purified, / having fashioned a golden lotus, one should worship [it], saying 'To Arka,'
with red oleander and a pair of red garments: / 'Just as the world is always free from sorrow by you alone, O Āditya,
so let there be freedom from sorrow for me, and devotion to you in every birth.' / Having worshipped in this manner on the sixth day, one should worship Brahmins with devotion.
Having himself consumed cow-urine, rising and performing his daily rites, / having diligently worshipped Brahmins, [he] together with a vessel of jaggery,
should present to a Brahmin a pair of fine garments and the lotus. / Having eaten food free of oil and salt on the seventh day while maintaining silence,
listening to the Purāṇa should then be performed by one desiring prosperity. / By this procedure, one should perform everything in both fortnights,
until the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha returns. / At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water jar accompanied by a golden lotus;
one should give a bed furnished with all accessories, and a brown cow rich in milk. / Whoever, free from deceit regarding wealth, performs the Viśokasaptamī
according to this procedure, goes to the supreme state. / For as long as one thousand lifetimes, plus a hundred million,
so long he does not encounter sorrow, freed from disease and misfortune. / Whatever desire he longs for, that he obtains in abundance.
Whoever performs it free from desire, however, goes to the supreme Brahman. / Whoever recites or even hears of this seventh day named Viśokā,
having attained the world of Indra, is never unhappy. / I shall declare yet another [vow] by the name of Phalasaptamī,
fasting upon which a man, freed from sins, shares in heaven. / In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, restrained in vows on the fifth day,
fasting on the sixth, having a golden lotus made, / one should give it along with sugar to a householder Brahmin.
And having fashioned a golden image of a single fruit, knowing dharma, / he should give it at twilight, saying: 'May Bhānu be pleased with me.'
Having worshipped the Brahmins according to his capacity, having eaten a meal of milk on the seventh day, / he should make an abstention from fruit until the seventh day of the dark fortnight.
Having fasted on that [day] according to rule, in this very sequence, / having likewise given a golden fruit accompanied by a golden lotus,
accompanied by a vessel of sugar and furnished with garments and garlands, / fasting on both seventh days according to this procedure for a year,
one should give [it] in succession, and utter the mantra of the Sun: / 'Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śukra, Hari, Śiva,
the glorious Vibhāvasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa—may [he] be pleased.' / Every month on the seventh day one should utter one name at a time.
Fortnight after fortnight, performing this, one should observe the abstention from fruit. / At the conclusion of the vow, one should worship a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments;
one should give a water jar filled with sugar, accompanied by a golden lotus and fruit: / 'Just as the desire of your devotees is never unfulfilled,
so may the attainment of endless fruit be mine birth after birth.' / Whoever performs this Phalasaptamī, which grants endless fruit,
delivers twenty-one generations of men, past and future. / Whoever hears or even recites it also shares in auspiciousness.
His self purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of the sun. / Whatever [sin], such as drinking liquor, was committed here or in the other world,
all that goes to destruction for one who performs the Phalasaptamī. / I shall likewise declare the Śarkarāsaptamī, which destroys taint,
by which endless longevity, health, and sovereignty are generated. / In the bright fortnight of Mādhava, restrained in vows on the seventh day,
having bathed in the morning with white sesame seeds, wearing pure garlands and unguents, / having drawn a lotus with saffron upon a bare patch of ground, complete with a pericarp,
one should offer fragrant ointment and flowers upon it, saying: 'Obeisance to Savitṛ.' / And one should set down a water jar accompanied by a vessel of sugar,
adorned with white garments, with white garlands and unguents, / furnished with a golden flower, and worship [it] with this mantra:
'Because you consist of all the Vedas, and you are recited in the Vedas, / you alone are the essence of immortality; therefore grant me peace.'
Then, having drunk the five products of the cow, one should sleep beside it on the ground, / remaining engaged in silently reciting the hymn to the Sun and listening to the Purāṇa.
After day and night have passed, performing his daily rites on the eighth day, / he should present all that to a Vedic scholar Brahmin.
He should feed Brahmins according to his capacity with sugar, clarified butter, and milk-rice; / he himself should also eat [food] without oil or salt, restrained in speech.
By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month. / At the end of the year, a bed accompanied by a water jar filled with sugar,
furnished with all accessories, as well as a single cow rich in milk; / and a capable person should give a house furnished with all accessories.
Or having fashioned [the lotus] with a thousand niṣkas, or with a hundred, / or with ten, or with three, or even with a single niṣka,
one should give the lotus according to one's capacity, with the recitation of the mantras as before. / One should not practice deceit regarding wealth; practicing it, one incurs defects.
Drops of nectar fell upon the earth from the mouth of the sun as he drank the nectar; / these became rice, mung beans, and sugarcane.
Therefore, the juice of sugar, the essence of sugarcane, is filled with the nature of nectar; / hence sugar is dear to the sun, holy in offerings to gods and ancestors.
And this Śarkarāsaptamī grants the fruit of a horse sacrifice, / calms all wickedness, and multiplies sons and grandsons.
Whoever performs it with supreme devotion attains the supreme Brahman; / he dwells in heaven for an eon, and then goes to the highest state.

O sinless one, whoever hears this, remembers it, or recites it here in the world of the lord of gods, / or even turns their mind to it, is honored by the gods and chief sages in the city of the immortals.
Hereafter, I shall likewise explain the Kamalasaptamī, / by the mere proclamation of which the sun is pleased in this world.
On the bright seventh lunar day of spring, well bathed with white mustard seeds, / and having placed an auspicious golden lotus in a vessel of sesame,
having covered it with a pair of garments, one should then worship it with perfumes and flowers, [saying]: / 'Obeisance to you who hold a lotus in your hand; obeisance to you who bear the universe;
obeisance to you, day-maker; obeisance to you, light-maker!' / Then, at twilight, accompanied by a jar of water,
having worshipped it with garments, garlands, and ornaments, one should give it to a Brahmin; / according to one's means, one should give a tawny cow, having adorned it according to the rule.
When the day and night have passed, one should then feed the Brahmins on the eighth lunar day, / and according to one's means one should eat food free of meat and devoid of oil.
By this rule, on the bright seventh lunar day month after month, / one should perform everything with devotion, free from dishonesty about one's wealth.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus,
and according to one's means one should give milch cows with gold; / one should give vessels, seats, lamps, and other desired implements.
Whoever performs the Kamalasaptamī by this rule / attains endless fortune and rejoices in the world of the sun.
Having gone in each eon to the seven worlds one by one, / surrounded by Apsarases, he then goes to the supreme state.

Whoever looks upon this, hears it for a moment, recites it with devotion, or even directs their mind [to it], / having obtained pure fortune here, also goes to the world of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sacred [vow] named Mandārasaptamī, / which destroys all sins and grants all desires.
On the fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, a man should eat light food; / then, having used a tooth-stick, the wise man should fast on the sixth.
Having worshipped Brahmins, he should pray to the mandāra tree at night; / then, having risen at dawn and bathed, he should again
feed Brahmins according to his means, and make eight mandāra flowers; / likewise a very handsome golden image of a man holding a lotus in his hand.
Having made an eight-petalled lotus of black sesamum seeds in a copper vessel, / [he should worship] with golden mandāra flowers, saying, 'To Bhāskara' in the east,
and likewise with a salutation, saying, 'To Sūrya' on the bright petal [in the south-east]; / likewise in the south, 'To Arka'; and likewise 'To Aryaman' in the south-west;
in the west, 'To the Abode of the Vedas'; and in the north-west, 'To Caṇḍabhānu'; / in the north, 'To Pūṣan' is to be worshipped; and then 'To Ānanda' [in the north-east];
and the male figure is to be placed in the pericarp, saying, 'To the Self of All'; / having wrapped it in white garments, with eatables, garlands, fruits, and the like,
having worshipped it thus, he should give it all to a knower of the Vedas. / The householder, restraining his speech, facing east, should eat without oil and salt.
By this rule, he should perform everything on the seventh lunar day month after month / for the duration of a year, free from dishonesty about his wealth.
And at the conclusion of the vow, having placed this very [gift] upon a water-pot, / it should be given along with cows according to one's wealth by one desiring prosperity, [saying]:
'Obeisance to the Lord of Mandāra, and to the Abode of Mandāra! / O Sun, carry us across from this ocean of cyclic existence!'
Whoever performs the Mandārasaptamī according to this rule / is freed from sin, becomes happy, and rejoices in heaven for an eon.
A man who walks in the night of cyclic existence, holding this lamp / against the terrible darkness of the mass of sins, does not stumble.
Whoever reads or even hears this Mandārasaptamī, / which grants the fruit of desired objects, is also freed from sins.
Now I shall tell of another auspicious vow, the Śubhasaptamī, / by fasting on which a person is freed from the flood of disease and grief.
Pure, having performed bathing and recitation of mantras in the holy month of Āśvayuja, / and having caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious words, he should then begin the Śubhasaptamī.
With devotion, he should worship a tawny cow with perfumes, garlands, and unguents, [saying]: / 'I bow to you, born of the sun, the abode of all the worlds;
to you, O auspicious, blessed one, for the purification of my body!' / Then, having prepared a prastha of sesame together with a copper vessel,
likewise a golden bull accompanied by garments, garlands, and raw sugar, / along with a pillow, a rest-vessel, and a seat,
accompanied by various kinds of fruits, eatables, ghee, and milk-rice, / he should give it at twilight, saying: 'May Aryaman be pleased!'
Having sipped the five products of the cow, he should sleep on the bare ground without a bed; / then, when morning comes, he should propitiate the Brahmins with devotion.
By this rule, a person should always give month after month / two garments, a golden bull, and likewise a cow made of gold.
At the end of a year, [he should give] a bed accompanied by sugarcane stalks and raw sugar, / a prastha of sesame in a copper vessel, and a golden bull;
he should give everything to a knower of the Vedas, saying, 'May the Soul of the Universe be pleased!' / The wise man who performs the Śubhasaptamī according to this rule,
his fortune and fame shall be spotless birth after birth. / Being worshipped in the abode of the gods by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas,
having become a lord of Gaṇas, he shall dwell until the dissolution of all beings; / and descended at the beginning of an eon, he shall become the lord of the seven continents.
This holy Śubhasaptamī is recited / as sufficient for the destruction of a thousand slayings of an embryo and a hundred slayings of a Brahmin.
Whoever reads this, hears it for a moment, or even sees it being given in connection with this, / their body freed here from all sin, they attain lordship over the Vidyādharas.

A person who performs for seven years the seventh-day vow endowed with seven regulations, / having sequentially become lord of the seven worlds, goes to the supreme state of Murāri.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Puṣkara-māhātmya of the first [part], the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

1.22.m: Bhīṣma said: / 'Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, / Tapoloka, and Satyaloka: these seven are proclaimed as the heavenly worlds.
How may sovereignty over all of them be attained in turn, / and in this world, auspicious beauty, long life, and health,
and abundant fortune, O Brahmin, worshipped by the gods?' / Pulastya said: / 'In ancient times, the Fire-god, along with the Wind-god, upon the earth,
was commanded by Puruhūta to destroy the enemies of the gods. / When thousands of Dānavas were burned by them then,
Tāraka, Kamalākṣa, Kāladaṃṣṭra, Parāvasu, / Virocana, and Saṃhrāda departed and lived there;
entering the middle of the ocean, they established an encampment. / Being [deemed] powerless, they were overlooked by Fire and Wind.'
From then on, having tormented the gods, / humans, serpents, and all the sages, they would enter the water again.
Thus, O king, for twelve thousand cosmic ages those heroes, / relying on the stronghold of the waters, tormented the three worlds.
Then, once again, the king of the gods commanded Fire and Wind: / "Let this reservoir of water be dried up without delay!
"Since this abode of Varuṇa is the refuge of our enemies, / therefore let it be brought to dryness by you two this very day!"
The two of them then said to Śakra, the slayer of Maya and Śambara: / "O lord of the gods, the destruction of the ocean is unrighteousness,
since the utter destruction of a great multitude of living beings would occur. / Therefore resort to another means, O Puraṃdara!
In only a single yojana of it, hundreds of millions of creatures / dwell, O excellent one; how does it deserve destruction?"
Addressed thus, the lord of the gods, his eyes blood-red with anger, / spoke these words in wrath to the immortals, Fire and Wind:
"Immortals never incur the connection with righteousness and unrighteousness; / you two especially stand as great-souled ones.
Since my command was not obeyed by you together with Wind, / taking a bodily form, devoted to the vow of a sage,
into a womb devoid of the treatises on dharma and material gain, O Fire! / Therefore, in a single form, in the guise of a sage among mortals,
your birth shall take place in the world together with Wind. / But when, even in human form, dried up as a mouthful of water by you
the ocean shall be, O Fire, then you will regain divinity!" / Thus, by Indra's curse, the two of them instantly fell to the surface of the earth.
They attained bodies, and their birth was from a water jar. / From the semen of Mitra and Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha was born as their son,
and then Agastya, of terrible austerities, the best of sages, arose. / From this brother he was indeed a brother, the sage being the younger brother of Vasiṣṭha.
Bhīṣma said: / And how are Mitra and Varuṇa remembered as his two fathers? / Tell now how Agastya's birth took place from a water jar.
Pulastya said: / Long ago, the ancient Puruṣa, Viṣṇu, becoming the son of Dharma, / once performed extensive austerities on Gandhamādana.
And terrified by his austerities, both Mādhava and the Bodiless One, / accompanied by a troop of Apsarases, were sent by Śakra to cause obstacles.
And when, by song, instrumental music, gestures, erotic sentiments and the like, Hari / could not be led into delusion by Kāma and Mādhava,
then the group of women of Kāma and Madhu fell into dejection. / Then, to dismay them, the elder brother of Nara
produced a woman from his thigh region, who enchanted even the three worlds. / The gods were captivated by her, and so were both of those deities.
Indeed, Hari said before the Apsarases and the gods: / "And this woman shall go by the name Urvaśī, renowned in the world."
Then, summoned by Mitra who was struck with desire, Urvaśī / was told, "Delight me!" and she said, "Very well."
Going then to the realm of the Sun, the lotus-eyed woman / was afterwards solicited by Varuṇa, and she spoke this word to him:
"I was chosen earlier by Mitra; the Sun is my lord, O master." / Varuṇa said: "Placing your mind in me, you may go."
When she had gone, saying "Very well," Mitra then uttered a curse: / "This very day go to the mortal world, to the son of the son of Soma,
and serve him, since this false dharma was performed by you!" / Then the semen was deposited into a water jar by Mitra and by Varuṇa.
Then the two best of sages were born. / Formerly, a king named Nimi was playing dice with women;
in the meantime, Vasiṣṭha, born of Brahmā, arrived. / The sage cursed the king, who did not offer him worship:
"May you become bodiless!" Cursed by him, that sage too was cursed by the king. / By their mutual curse, the luminous energies of both became disembodied;
for the removal of the curse, they went to Brahmā, the lord of the universe. / Then, by Brahmā's command, Nimi took up residence in the eyes,
and the winking of people's eyes came to be for his rest, O king. / And Vasiṣṭha also was born in that water jar, just as before.
Then Agastya was born, four-armed, with a rosary and a water pot; / with a tranquil mind, he became the best of ṛṣis.
On one part of the Malaya mountain, according to the Vaikhānasa rule, / accompanied by his wife and surrounded by brāhmaṇas, he performed exceedingly difficult austerities.
Then, after a great span of time, seeing the world tormented by Tāraka and others, / he angrily drank up the abode of Varuṇa.
Then Śaṃkara and the others all became granters of boons to him; / Lord Brahmā and Viṣṇu came to bestow boons:
"Choose a boon, welfare to you, whatever is desired here, O sage!" / Agastya said: / "For as long as twenty-five crores of thousands of Brahmās endure,
I shall be a rider of celestial chariots in the pathway of the southern sky. / Whoever performs worship of me from the rising of my chariot,
shall become the sovereign of the seven worlds in succession. / And whoever proclaims an ashram at Puṣkara by my name,
may he attain sacredness; this is the boon chosen by me! / Those who will perform a śrāddha here with devotion, preceded by funeral rice-balls,
all their ancestral hosts, residing in heaven together with me, / shall abide for this length of time; this indeed is my boon."
"So be it!" they said, and the gods departed as they had come. / Therefore, an offering of water should always be given to Agastya by the wise.
Bhīṣma said: / How should the offering of water be made to that sage? / Tell me the procedure in the worship of Agastya.
Pulastya said: / At dawn, or at night upon his rising, a wise householder / should take a bath with white sesame seeds, wearing white garlands and garments.
He should set up a flawless jar, adorned with garlands and cloth, / furnished with the five gems, along with a vessel of ghee.
Placing a golden figure of a man of the size of a thumb, with long staff-like arms / and four hands, upon the mouth of the jar, together with seven heaps of grain,

along with a bell-metal vessel and white unhusked barley-grains, having raised the long-armed figure upon the jar, / he should give it with the mantra to an eminent twice-born man, with single-minded attention, facing the direction of Yama.

And if he has the capacity, a man, having bowed, should give a white cow to the twice-born man, / one having silver hooves, a golden face, accompanied by her calf, rich in milk, adorned with garlands, cloths, and bells.
From the rising of this [star] for seven nights, O king, all this should be given by a man, / or until seventeen years have passed; moreover, some say even beyond that.
"Resembling the kāśa flower, born of Fire and Wind, / son of Mitra and Varuṇa, jar-born one, salutation to you!"
And thus renouncing a fruit each year, he does not suffer; / having performed a fire sacrifice, the person may subsequently consume the fruit.
The man who offers the water-offering according to this rite / attains this world, which grants the fruits of beauty and freedom from disease.
With the second, he attains the atmosphere; and beyond that, the realm of heaven; / whoever gives seven water-offerings attains indeed the seven worlds.
He who recites or hears properly this deed and witnesses the worship of Agastya, / and even gives his mind [to it], goes to the abode of Viṣṇu and is worshipped by the hosts of immortals.
Bhīṣma said: / Tell me, O highly intelligent one, of that which grants the fruit of good fortune and health, destroys enemies, / and bestows enjoyment and liberation.
Pulastya said: / What the slayer of Andhaka formerly told Umā, O king, / when delightful stories about dharma had begun,
that I shall now proclaim, which grants the fruit of enjoyment and liberation. / Gaurī said: / A curse was indeed given to me and Lakṣmī by Sāvitrī, O lord of the gods.
Tell me how I may attain preeminence like Lakṣmī. / Śaṃkara said: / Listen attentively, O goddess, to another [observance] similarly established by myself,
an unsurpassed worship for men and women: / in the month of Nabhasya, or in Vaiśākha, or in the auspicious Mārgaśirṣa,
on the third day of the bright fortnight, having bathed with yellow mustard seeds, / yellow orpiment mixed with cow urine, cow milk, and ghee,
and curd mixed with sandalwood, one should place a mark on the forehead; / for it brings good fortune and health, and is ever pleasing to Lalitā.
On the third day of every fortnight, a man or a married woman / should wear red garments and white flowers.
A widow, however, should wear only a single white garment, / and an unmarried girl should put on two fine white garments.
One should bathe the goddess with the five products of the cow, then with pure milk, / likewise with honey, and then with fragrant flower-water.
One should worship her with white flowers and diverse kinds of fruits, / accompanied by grains, parched rice and the like, salt, jaggery, milk, and ghee.
You must always worship the goddess with white unhusked rice and sesame seeds; / O fair-faced one, one should worship the two feet every fortnight:
"Homage to the Granter of Boons," [worshipping] the two feet; likewise, "Homage to Śrī," the two ankles; / "Homage to Aśokā," the two shanks; and "To Pārvatī," the two knees;
the two thighs "To the Bringer of Auspiciousness"; likewise, the waist "To Vāmadevī"; / the belly "To Padmodarā"; and "Homage to Śrī" at the throat;
the two hands "To the Bestower of Fortune"; the two arms "To the Glory of the Fair-Faced One"; / the mouth "To the Destroyer of Pride"; and the smile "To the Inspier of Love";
likewise, "Homage to Gaurī," the nose; and "To Utpalā," the two eyes; / the forehead "To Tuṣṭi"; the curl of hair and the head "Homage to Kātyāyanī";
"Homage to Gaurī, homage to Puṣṭi, homage to Kānti, homage to Śrī, / homage, homage to Rambhā, to Lalitā, and to Vāmadevī."
Having thus worshipped in accordance with the rules, one should draw a lotus in front, / endowed with sixteen petals in due order and with a pericarp.
In the east one should place Gaurī, and next to her Aparṇā; / likewise Bhavānī in the south, and next to her Rudrāṇī;
one should place Saumyā, living in passion, in the western quarter; / Pāṭalā in the northwest; Ugrā and Umā in the north;
Sādhyā, Pathyā, likewise Saumyā, Maṅgalā, Kumadā, Satī, / and Bhadrā; and placing Lalitā in the middle upon the pericarp,
one should assign them with flowers, unhusked grains, water, or prostration. / Having caused auspicious songs and music to sound, one should worship
a married woman with red garments, red garlands, and ointments; / and one should scatter vermilion and bath-powder upon their heads;
for vermilion, saffron, and bathing are exceedingly dear [to her]. / Likewise, one should diligently honor the teacher who gave the instruction;
where the guru is not worshipped, there all rites are fruitless. / And one should worship Gaurī constantly with prayers and dark blue lotuses.
In the month of Kārtika, O beloved, she should be worshipped diligently with scarlet bandhujīva flowers; / with jasmine flowers in Mārgaśirṣa; with yellow kuraṇṭaka flowers in Pauṣa;
in Māgha a person should worship the goddess with kunda and white water lilies; / in Phālguna one should worship her with sinduvāra or jasmine;
in Caitra with mallikā and aśoka flowers; in Vaiśākha with fragrant pāṭala flowers; / in Jyeṣṭha with lotus and mandāra flowers; in Āṣāḍha with water lilies;
in Śrāvaṇa one should always worship her with mandāra or mālatī flowers. / Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water with kuśa grass,
a bilva leaf, arka flowers, a lotus, and water from a cow's horn, / the five products of the cow, and a bilva [fruit]—one should consume these in due order, continuously.
This consumption is declared to begin in the month of Bhādrapada. / And on the third day of every fortnight, O fair-faced one,
having fed a married couple, one should worship them devotedly with garments, garlands, and unguents. / One should give two yellow garments to the man, and two silk garments to the woman;
to the woman one should give niṣpāva beans, cumin, salt, together with sugarcane stalks and jaggery; / and to the man, a fruit together with a golden blue lotus.
"Just as the god never departs, abandoning you, O goddess, / so deliver me from the boundless ocean of worldly existence and sorrow!"
[Saying:] "Kumudā, Vimalā, Ānandā, Bhavānī, Vasudhā, Śivā, / Lalitā, Kamalā, Gaurī, Satī, Rambhā, and Pārvatī—
may she be pleased!" in the months beginning with Nabhasya. / At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus.
One should worship twenty-four couples, or twelve, / or eight, or eight more; or one should worship in the fourth month.
Having first given to the guru, one should then worship the others. / This Anantatṛtīyā has been declared, which always yields infinite fruit.
It removes all sins, O goddess, and increases good fortune and health; / nor should one ever violate it out of stinginess.
Whether a man or a woman, one should observe the vow of fasting: / a pregnant woman, a woman in confinement, a maiden, or a sick woman [may eat] at night.
When she is impure, then she should have it performed by another while being self-restrained herself. / Whoever observes this third-day vow that grants endless fruit
is exalted in the world of Śiva for a full hundred crores of kalpas. / Even one devoid of wealth should fast as long as a year;
by the method of flowers and mantras, he too attains that same fruit. / Or whatever woman performs it desiring her own welfare
attains a male birth brought about by Gaurī's grace. / Whoever recites or hears this vow of the mountain's daughter dwells in Indra's realm,
and whoever inspires devotion to it is worshipped by the gods, celestial women, and kinnaras. / I shall declare another third-day vow that destroys sins,
known as Rasakalyāṇī, which the wise know originated in a previous kalpa. / Having reached the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
one should bathe in the morning with fragrant unguents, milk, and sesame seeds; / one should bathe the goddess with honey, and likewise with sugarcane juice,
and again with fragrant water, and worship her with saffron. / Having worshipped the right limbs, one should then worship the left limbs:
the goddess's foot "To Lalitā," and then one should worship the two left ankles; / the shanks and knee "To Śānti," and likewise the thigh "Homage to Śrī";
the waist "To Madālasā," and the belly "To Amalā"; / the two breasts "To Madanavāsinī," and the neck "To Kumudā";
the arm and forearm "To Mādhavī," and "To Kamalā," O sweetly smiling one; / the eyebrow and forehead "To Rudrāṇī," and the curl of hair "To Śaṃkarā";
the forehead "To Madanā," and the two eyebrows "To Mohanā"; / the two eyes "To the Bearer of the Crescent Moon," and the face "To Tuṣṭi."
'Homage to Utkaṇṭhinī,' the neck; 'Homage to Amṛtā,' the body; / and 'To Rambhā,' the mighty arms; 'Homage to Viśokā,' the two hands;
the chest to her named Manmathā; likewise the belly to Pāṭalā; / the waist to Suratavāsinī; likewise the thighs to Paṅkajaśrī;
the knees and shanks with 'Homage to Gaurī'; and likewise one should worship the ankles 'To Śānti'; / the two feet to Dharādharā; and the head with 'Homage to Viśvakāyā';
'Homage to Bhavānī, to Kāminī, to Vāsudevī, the fortune of the world; / to Ānandadā, to Nandā, to Subhadrā, homage, homage.'
Having thus worshipped according to the rite, he should worship a twice-born husband and wife, / having fed them with sweet food, being free from envy.
Giving a water-pot with sweetmeats, two pairs of white garments, / [and] a golden lotus, he should then worship them with perfumes and garlands.
[Saying:] 'May Kumudā be pleased here,' he should undertake the vow of salt. / By this rite he should always worship the goddess month by month.
He should avoid salt in Māgha, and again molasses in Phālguna; / likewise butter should be avoided in Caitra, and honey in Mādhava;
water in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and likewise cumin in Āṣāḍha; / in Śrāvaṇa he should avoid milk, and curd likewise in Bhādrapada;
ghee in Āśvayuja, and likewise honey must be avoided in Ūrja; / coriander in Mārgaśīrṣa, and sugar must be avoided in Pauṣa.
At the end of the vow in each and every month, he should give a water-pot full of these / at evening time, along with a dish of eatables:
laḍḍus and sevikās, and saṃyāva, then pūrikās, / nārikās filled with ghee, and piṣṭa-filled nandikīs,
milk-vegetables and curd-rice, and likewise piṇḍa-vegetables; / beginning with Māgha, he should offer these in order upon the water-pot.
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Rambhā, Subhadrā, and Śivā, Jayā, / Lalitā, Kamalā, Anaṅgā, Maṅgalā, Ratilālasā—
in order, during the months beginning with Māgha, he should proclaim: 'May [she] be pleased!' / In all cases, the consumption of pañcagavya is prescribed.
He should continuously fast; if unable, eating at night is permitted. / A woman should thus perform this Rasakalyāṇinī vow.
When Māgha arrives again, upon a jar of sugar, / having made a golden Gaurī, endowed with the five jewels,
the size of one's own thumb, with a rosary and water-pot, / four-armed, adorned with the moon, and covered in a fine white cloth—
likewise a pair of cattle of gold, white garments, / and a vessel with clothing, he should give, saying: 'May Bhavānī be pleased.'
Whoever performs the Rasakalyāṇinī vow according to this rite / is immediately freed from all sins.
Through a thousand rebirths he is never born miserable; / he obtains whatever fruit is attained by a thousand Agniṣṭomas.
Whatever woman performs it, whether an unmarried girl, O fair-faced one, / or a poor widow, she also shares in that fruit.
Endowed with good fortune and health, she is honoured in Gaurī's world. / Whoever reads this thus, or hears it on occasion, / freed from all impurities, goes to Pārvatī's world.
And whoever sets his mind upon it for the good of men, / will go unfailingly to the world of the lord of the gods. / Just so I shall proclaim another sin-destroying third [tithi]
known throughout the world by name, this foremost delight-maker. / When upon the bright third [tithi] the Āṣāḍha asterism occurs at any time,
or the asterism of Brahmā, or Maghā, Hasta, or even Mūla, / one should then perform a full bath with fragrant darbha-water.
Wearing white garlands and garments, anointed with white fragrant paste, / he should worship Bhavānī with devotion, using fragrant white flowers,
and Mahādeva, complete, seated upon a great seat: / 'Homage to Vāsudevī,' the two feet; 'Homage to Śaṅkara,' [the feet] of Hari;
the shanks to the destroyer of grief, and 'Homage to the giver of honor,' of the Lord; / he should worship the thighs to Rambhā, and to Śiva, wielder of the Pināka;
the waist to Ānandinī of the goddess, and to the trident-holder who bears a trident in his hand; / likewise the navel to Mādhavī, and to Bhava, Śambhu;
the breasts to the cause of delight, and to Śaṅkara who bears the moon; / 'Homage to Utkaṇṭhinī,' the neck, and to Nīlakaṇṭha, Hari;
the two hands to the bearer of the blue lotus, and to Rudra, the lord of the world; / and the two arms to Parirambhiṇī, and to Hari who delights in dance;
the face of the goddess to Vilāsinī, and to the bull [rider], the all-pervading lord; / and the smile to Smaraṇīyā, and to the omnipresent whose face is the universe;
the eyes to Mandāravāsinī, and to the trident-holder whose abode is the universe; / and the brows to Nṛtyapriyā, and to Śambhu who bears the noose and trident;
the forehead of the goddess to Indrāṇī, and to the all-pervading bull-rider; / the crown of the goddess to Svāhā, and to the bearer of the Gaṅgā;
having universal bodies, universal arms, universal feet and faces, the auspicious couple— / I bow to the gracious bestowers of boons, Pārvatī and Parameśvara.
Having worshipped thus according to the rite, in front of the two auspicious ones / he should then make lotuses and water-lilies with powders of various colours,
a conch, a discus with an outer rim, [and] an auspicious svastika. / As many particles of the powder as fall upon the ground there,
for that many thousands of years he is honoured in Śiva's world. / Four vessels of ghee, with gold according to one's capacity,
having given to a twice-born, along with a water-pot filled with water, / he should offer these every fortnight for four months.
Then for four months, as before, upon the water-pot / [he should offer] four vessels of ghee, and afterwards vessels of sesame.
Fragrant water, flower-water, sandalwood, saffron-water, / unboiled milk and curd, and water from a cow's horn,
lotus-water, and water mixed with kuṣṭha-powder, / vetiver-water, and water mixed with barley-powder,
and having sipped sesame-water, he should sleep in the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa; / sipping for two fortnights [each] is prescribed.
White flowers are praised everywhere in constant worship; / and at the time of gift, he should utter this mantra everywhere:
'May Gaurī ever be pleased with me, Maṅgalā for the destruction of sin, / may Lalitā be for good fortune, Bhavānī for all attainment.'
At the end of the year, [he should offer] salt with molasses and saffron, / a jar with sandalwood, along with a golden lotus;
a golden [image] for the pleasure of Umā, accompanied by fruits in that direction, / [and] he should present a bed with bedding, coverings, and a bolster,
to a brāhmaṇa along with his wife, saying: 'May Gaurī be pleased with me.' / A person will attain the prosperity named Ātmānandakarī;
endowed with long life and joy, he will never meet with grief. / Whatever woman performs it, whether an unmarried girl or a widow,
she also obtains that fruit, cherished by the goddess's grace. / Fasting thus every fortnight according to the rite of worship with mantras,
one attains the world of the Rudras, from which return is hard to obtain. / Whoever hears this daily or recites it with devotion,
Having gone to Śakra's world, he is honored, remaining there for a kalpa. / Śaṃkara said: / If a woman is devoted to such an observance,
then what is the curse of that poor Sāvitrī? / There is no calculation of it, since the most beautiful woman of the three worlds,
She too was venerable before, and she was Lakṣmī, received by Viṣṇu. / Long ago, for your sake, I destroyed the sacrifice of Dakṣa.

And formerly the ocean was churned by Viṣṇu for the sake of Lakṣmī.
I am the servant of both of you; do not feel fear anywhere.

Sāvitrī, being angry, must be honored and propitiated
by me, by Viṣṇu, and by Brahmā who desires respect.

I will go to Brahmā's abode, and you stay here, fair-faced lady."
Having spoken thus, Rudra went; Gaurī remained there.

For the entire Kṛta age, in that sacrifice, the fire-god,
carrying the oblations of the gods, pleased the three worlds.

The Lord gave food to the foremost brahmins, pleasures to the host of Vidyādharas,
and the attainment of desires to human beings—all indeed he granted.

Viṣṇu was then addressed by Rudra: "Do you proclaim your duties,
the duties of Gaurī, and the vow of Sarasvatī that has been described."
When it was spoken thus by Rudra, Viṣṇu spoke with respect: / "I shall not proclaim my own dharma now, O Śaṅkara."

You must declare my glorification, O best of gods.
Indeed, it was spoken by you before, and in the Kṛta age the destruction of sins [will occur].

It will happen, there is no doubt, and you will become purified."
Bhīṣma said:
"By what vow does speech become sweet, O best of sages,

and likewise good fortune among people, intelligence, knowledge, good skill,
harmony in marriage, and union with relatives,

and long life for men? Tell me that, O best of men."
Pulastya said:
"You have asked well, O king. Hear the vow of Sarasvatī,

by the mere recitation of which goddess Sarasvatī is pleased.
As long as a devotee recites this unexcelled hymn and vow,

having worshipped first at the beginning of the day, he should commence the divine hymn,
or on a Sunday, when the planets and lunar mansions are favorable.

He should feed milk-rice to the brahmins and cause Brahmā's blessings to be uttered,
having given white garments and gold according to his capacity.

He should worship Gāyatrī with devotion using white garlands and ointments:
'Just as, O goddess, the blessed Brahmā, grandfather of the worlds,

does not abandon you and remain [without you], so be the granter of boons to me.
Whatever Vedas, scriptures, dharmas, dancing, singing, and so forth exist,

are not devoid of you, O goddess; thus may accomplishments be mine.
Lakṣmī, Medhā, Dharā, Puṣṭi, Gaurī, Tuṣṭi, Jayā, Mati—

protect me, O Sarasvatī, with these eight forms of yours!'
Having thus worshipped Gāyatrī, who holds a lute and a lotus,

with white flowers and unbroken rice with devotion, and who carries a water pot and a book,
the knower of dharma should eat with a vow of silence in the evening and morning.

And on the fifth day of each fortnight, [he should give] an auspicious cow to a brahmin,
and likewise a prastha of rice grains along with a vessel of ghee,

milk, and gold, saying: 'May Gāyatrī be pleased!'
And at twilight he should maintain silence, practicing this.

He should not eat at night as long as thirteen months [last].
When the vow is completed, he should give food made with white rice grains,

a divine canopy and a bell, furnished with a white silken cloth,
sandalwood, a pair of garments, and delicious curd-rice.

Then he should also worship with devotion the guru who instructed him,
free from stinginess with wealth, with garments, garlands, and ointments.

He who performs the vow of Sarasvatī according to this rule
becomes endowed with good fortune and intelligence, and has a sweet voice.

By the grace of Sarasvatī he is honored in the world of Brahmā.
A woman who performs it also partakes of that fruit.

He resides in the world of Brahmā, O king, for thirty thousand kalpas.
He who hears or reads the vow of Sarasvatī,

He too would dwell in the city of the Vidyādharas for thirty thousand years.

1.23.m:
Bhīṣma said:
"Those Vaiṣṇava dharmas that Rudra proclaimed here,
tell me about them, O chief of brahmins: what are they like, and what is their fruit?"

Pulastya said:
"Formerly in the Rathaṃtara kalpa, the great-souled Pināka-wielding Mahādeva
residing on Mount Mandara was questioned by Brahmā himself:

'How may health and unending sovereignty, O lord of immortals,
and permanent liberation for men come about by little austerity, O god?

What is that knowledge, O Mahādeva, through your grace, O Adhokṣaja,
by which, even with slight austerity, a great fruit is spoken of here?'
Thus questioned by Brahmā, the universal self and creator of the worlds, / the lord of Umā spoke these words that cause delight to the mind:

The Lord said:
'When, after this Rathaṃtara kalpa, there will be the twentieth kalpa,
called Vārāha, then in the auspicious manvantara,

the seventh known as Vaivasvata, when it arrives, O upholder of the seven worlds,
in the age called Dvāpara, when it is the twenty-seventh,

at its end, Vāsudeva Janārdana of great splendor,
Viṣṇu, will become threefold in order to relieve the burden [of the earth]:

sage Dvaipāyana there, then the son of Rohiṇī, and Keśava—
Keśava, the enemy of Kaṃsa, slayer of Keśin, destroyer of distress.

The city named Dvāravatī, which is presently Kuśasthalī,
endowed with divine power, as a dwelling for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,

Tvaṣṭṛ, by the order of that Lord of the universe, will then build, O Brahmā.
Once, sitting in that assembly, he of boundless brilliance,

accompanied by wives, learned Vṛṣṇis, numerous men of generous gifts,
Kurus, gods, and Gandharvas, the crusher of Kaiṭabha,

when ancient stories connected with dharma had commenced,
the majestic one will be questioned by Bhīmasena.

Seeing differences, he will explain that dharma questioned by you,
and then, O Brahmā, that Vṛkodara will be the performer.

The mighty son of Pāṇḍu is the promoter of this dharma,
in whose belly there is the fierce sacrificial-fire named Vṛka.

Therefore that righteous-souled one is addressed as Vṛkodara.
He is extremely fond of tasty food, great, with the strength of ten thousand elephants.

Though righteous, he is unable to fast because of his fierce fire [of digestion].
Because this vow is greater than all vows,

Vāsudeva, the Soul of all and teacher of the universe, will proclaim it,
giving the fruit of all sacrifices, destroying all sins,

calming all evils, worshipped by all gods,
the purest of the pure, the most auspicious of auspicious things,
the future of future things, and the most ancient of purāṇas.'

Vāsudeva said:
'If on the eighth, fourteenth, and twelfth days, O Bhārata,
and on other days and asterisms you are not able to fast,

then, fasting on this foremost lunar day that destroys sin, O Bhīma,
by this rule, you will go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

When the tenth day of the bright half of the month of Māgha arrives,
then, having anointed himself with ghee, he should bathe with sesame seeds.

Likewise, he should worship Viṣṇu, saying, "Homage to Nārāyaṇa!",
and worship the feet saying, "To Kṛṣṇa!", and the head saying, "To the soul of Kṛṣṇa!",

the chest saying, "To Vaikuṇṭha!", to the bearer of Śrīvatsa,
to the bearer of the conch, mace, and discus, the giver of boons.

Having thus worshipped Nārāyaṇa in the order of invocation,
[he should worship] the belly saying, "To Dāmodara!", and the waist saying, "To Pañcajana!"

[Saying:] 'To the Lord of Fortune', [he worships] the thighs; 'To the Bearer of Beings', the knees;
'Homage to Nīla', the shanks; and again, 'To the Enjoyer of All', the feet.

'Homage to the Goddess, homage to Tranquility, homage to Lakṣmī, homage to Śrī,
homage to Satisfaction, homage to Nourishment, homage to Resolve, homage to Dawn! Homage, homage!'

'Homage to the Lord of Birds, swift as the wind, the winged one,
to the Destroyer of Poison'—saying this, he should worship Garuḍa.

Having thus worshipped Govinda, Umā's husband, and Vināyaka
with perfumes, garlands, incenses, and also with various kinds of foods,

and having eaten kṛsarā [rice and pulses] moistened with cow's milk, or sweet milk-rice
together with ghee, he then goes to another place.

Taking a tooth-stick made of banyan or khadira wood, the wise man,
having sipped water, facing east or north, should clean his teeth.

Having performed the evening twilight rite after the sun has set, he should say:
'Homage to Nārāyaṇa! I have taken refuge in you.'

'Fasting on the eleventh [lunar day] and having worshipped Keśava
who lies on the serpent couch, remaining [awake] that entire night,

having offered with ghee to the All-Consuming [Fire] along with eminent brāhmaṇas,
I will break my fast with milk on the twelfth [lunar day], O Lotus-Eyed One!

May this [vow] of mine be accomplished without obstacle according to my wish.'
Having spoken thus, he should sleep on the ground, and having listened again to legendary history,

when morning comes, O lord of the people, he should go to the river,
