bathe with joy, and in the same way strictly avoid heretics.

Having attended to the twilight rite according to rule and having performed the libation to the ancestors,
and having bowed down to Hṛṣīkeśa reclining on the serpent couch,

in front of his house the wise man should have a pavilion erected with devotion;
he should make an auspicious altar four cubits [in size], O crusher of foes.

He should erect there an archway measuring four cubits,
and in the center an earthen pot provided with an aperture the size of a māṣa bean,

filled with water; sitting below upon a black antelope skin,
he should receive its stream on his head for the entire night.

The knowers of the Veda know that great fruit comes from abundant streams;
therefore, O best of the Kurus, a restrained twice-born should have it done.

To the south he should make [a hearth] in the shape of a half-moon, to the west round,
and to the north shaped like an aśvattha leaf;

in the center, the twice-born Vaiṣṇava should make one shaped like a lotus.
Standing on the eastern platform, he should not arrange [it] in the south.

Devoted to Viṣṇu, he should sustain the stream of water on his head.
A second platform is for the deity, and there a lotus with its pericarp;

in its center he should install the god, Puruṣottama.
Having made there a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit, with three girdles,

and having a vulva-shaped mouth, in that [fire] brāhmaṇas should offer
barley, ghee, and sesame into the fire with mantras addressed to the deity Viṣṇu.

Having properly performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, he should arrange [the offerings] there;
he should carefully pour a stream of clarified butter into the middle pit.

[He should direct] a stream of milk onto the God of gods, and a stream of water over himself;
he should cause a stream of clarified butter, measuring half a niṣpāva bean, to fall.

According to his wish, [he continues] the uninterrupted [streams] of milk and water throughout the night.
Having set up thirteen water jars, O man of great strength,

furnished with various foods and adorned with white cloths,
and having placed over them udumbara vessels provided with the five gems,

the burnt-offering is to be performed by four Ṛgvedic priests facing north,
and the chanting of the Rudra hymns by four priests devoted to the Yajurveda,

and the Vaiṣṇava sāmans by four Sāmavedic priests.
In this way, he should worship the twelve brāhmaṇas with garments, garlands, ointments,

finger-rings, bracelets, gold threads,
garments, and beds, free from deceit regarding wealth.

Thus the night is to be spent with sounds of song and auspicious [instruments];
and for the preceptor, everything should be double.

Then, rising up at clear daybreak, O best of the Kurus,
thirteen cows are to be given, adorned with gold horns,

giving abundant milk, of gentle temper, accompanied by bronze milking vessels,
with silver hooves, accompanied by their calves, and smeared with sandalwood.

Having given those [cows] to them and having satisfied
all the brāhmaṇas with varied food and drink, and likewise with various umbrellas,

and having himself eaten non-alkaline and saltless [food], he should dismiss them.
Having followed eight steps along with his sons and wife,

[saying:] 'May the Lord of gods, Keśava, the destroyer of distress, be pleased with this!'
Thus, by the preceptor's instruction, the wise man should send the jars, the cows, the beds,

and the garments to the houses of all of them.
In the absence of many beds, even one well-prepared

bed furnished with all accessories the householder should give, O Bhīma.
Having caused the legendary histories and Purāṇas to be recited, he should spend

that day, O tiger among the Kurus, if he desires vast fortune.
Therefore, resorting to firmness and free from envy, Bhīmasena,

duly perform this secret vow spoken by me out of affection.
When performed by you, O hero, it will also be known by your name;

for this auspicious Bhīmadvādaśī removes all sins;
in former eons it is recited under the name Kalyāṇinī.

You will be the first author [of it] in this Boar eon, O supreme among great heroes,
by remembering and celebrating which the sin of the ruler of the gods was entirely destroyed.

Having seen her who was desired by the apsarases, in other births she was made a courtesan;
then, though born in a vaiśya family, she was born as Puloman's daughter, the wife of Puruhūta [Indra].

Even there she was a servant; she is now my beloved Satyabhāmā.
This very auspicious rite was performed formerly by the daughter of a twice-born, who became Vedavatī.

And on this auspicious lunar day, Vivasvat, having a thousand rays,
was bathed in former times with a thousand streams, attained that radiant orb, and became the lord of planets.

This very [rite] was performed by great deities headed by Mahendra and by millions of gods and demons;
its fruit cannot be fully told here, even if there were ten million tongues in one's mouth.

Even the son of the lord of the Yādavas will recount it as destroying the impurities of the Kali [age] and infinite;
and it is indeed capable of delivering ancestors gone to hell for one who performs it here.

Whoever, sinless, hears this, recites it with devotion, or reads it here for the sake of helping others,
becomes devoted to the Lotus-Navel here and attains honor from Śakra [Indra].

The twelfth [lunar day] which in former creation was named Kalyāṇinī, to be worshipped in the bright half of Māgha,
will be performed by the son of Pāṇḍu, of infinite merit, sinless, bearing the name Bhīma.

Brahmā said:
The origin of the castes and stages of life has been heard by me in the Purāṇas,
as well as good conduct, O Lord, through the extensive branches of the treatises on dharma.

I desire to hear truly about the proper conduct of courtesans.
Īśvara said:
In that very city, O Brahmā, sixteen thousand

women of Vāsudeva will exist, O lotus-born one.
With them, in springtime, crowded with cuckoos and swarms of bees,

in a flowering park on the bank of a lake of blossoming white water-lilies,
fully adorned along with his praiseworthy wives,
The soul of the universe, Kṛṣṇa, the uplifter of the Yadu race, / deer-eyed, glorious, wearing a crown of jasmine flowers, will delight [them].
Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, walking along the nearby road, / appearing as the god of love himself, adorned with all ornaments,
was looked upon with longing by those women afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god. / When desire was awakened in their minds,
perceiving that with his eye of meditation, the omniscient Lord of the Universe, / the Master himself, will say to them: “Robbers shall carry you away!
Since this tender thought was entertained so openly!” / Then, propitiated by them, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow will say this:
To those women distressed by the curse, the Lord, the source of all beings, / the deliverer of fishermen who took refuge in the north, who is dear to brāhmaṇas,
whose self is infinite, will instruct them in what brings future welfare: / “The sage Dālbhya will explain a vow to you.”
Having spoken thus and abandoned them, the Lord vanished. / Then, after a great length of time, when the burden [of the earth] was removed,
when the destruction by iron clubs was concluded, when Keśava had departed to heaven, / when the Yadu race was emptied, and when Arjuna was defeated by bandits,
when Kṛṣṇa’s wives were abducted and enjoyed by fishermen, / and when they stayed at Arbuda, tormented by misery, O four-faced one [Brahmā],
the great ascetic named Dālbhya, whose self is fixed in yoga, will arrive. / Having honored him with respectful water and prostrated repeatedly,
lamenting profusely, their eyes clouded with tears, / remembering various enjoyments, celestial garlands and ointments,
their husband, the infinite and invincible Lord of the worlds, / and the city of divine majesty with houses of various gems,
and all the residents of Dvārakā, the god-like young men, / standing before the sage, they will ask this question:
“O venerable one, all of us have been enjoyed by force by robbers. / We have fallen from our own dharma; in this, you are our refuge.
Long ago, O brāhmaṇa, you were instructed by the wise Keśava. / How is it that, having attained union with the Lord, we have become courtesans?
Tell us, O rich in asceticism, what the duty of courtesans is.” / I shall recount what Dālbhya Caikitāyana said to them.
Dālbhya said: / “Long ago, while you were sporting in water in Lake Mānasa, / proud as you were, Nārada came near you.
Long ago, all of you were daughters of the Fire-god, apsarases. / Without bowing, out of arrogance, you questioned that knower of yoga:
‘Instruct us how Nārāyaṇa may become our husband.’ / Therefore, both a boon and this curse were granted long ago:
‘By gifting two beds in the months of Madhu and Mādhava, / furnished with gold utensils, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
surely Nārāyaṇa will become your husband in another birth. / Because without bowing to me, out of pride in your beauty and good fortune,
you questioned me, therefore separation will soon come to you. / Carried off by robbers, all of you will become courtesans.’
Thus, through the curse of Nārada and through the curse of Keśava, / you have all become courtesans, deluded by desire.
Now listen to what I shall say, O fair ladies: / Long ago, in the war between the gods and asuras, when by the hundreds the gods had slain
the Dānavas, asuras, Daityas, and Rākṣasas here and there, / their thousands of wives, in hundreds and in thousands,
those who were married and those who had been enjoyed by force— / to all of them the Lord of the gods, the best of speakers, said:
‘Live now according to the way of courtesans in the palace of the king / and in temples, full of devotion, O fair-hipped women!
You shall obtain a livelihood from the king and from your master, / and good fortune will attend all of you according to your capacity.
Whoever comes to your home offering a fee, / must always be attended without deceit, with sincere, affectionate feelings.
When an auspicious day for the deities and the ancestors arrives, / cows, land, gold, and grain should be given according to one’s means.
And the vow that I shall teach you, perform it in every detail; / the knowers of the Veda know this to be sufficient for crossing over the cycle of rebirth.
When Sunday coincides with Hasta, Puṣya, or Punarvasu, / a woman should properly take a bath with all medicinal herbs.
Then Hari, whose essence is the five-arrowed god of love, will come near. / One should worship the lotus-eyed one with praises of the god of love:
Worshipping the feet with ‘Homage to Kāma,’ the shanks with ‘Homage to the infatuating one,’ / the penis with ‘Homage to the treasure of love,’ the hips with ‘Homage to the lover,’
[he offered] the navel to the ocean of joy, the belly to Vāmana, / the heart to the Lord of the Heart, and the two breasts to the one who brings delight.
the neck with ‘Homage to longing,’ the face with ‘Homage to the giver of joy,’ / the left shoulder with ‘Homage to the flower-bowed one,’ the right with ‘Homage to the flower-arrowed one,’
the garland with ‘Homage to the mind-born one,’ the hair with ‘Homage to the trembling one,’ / and likewise the head with ‘Homage to the self of all,’ one should worship the God of gods:
‘Homage to the auspicious one, to the tranquil one, to the holder of the noose and goad, / to the mace-bearer, the one clad in yellow garments, the bearer of the conch and discus;
Homage to Nārāyaṇa, homage to the embodiment of Kāmadeva; / homage to Śānti, homage to Prīti, homage to Rati, homage to Śrī;
Homage to Puṣṭi, homage to Tuṣṭi, homage to the attainment of all goals.’ / Having thus worshipped Govinda, the Lord whose essence is the bodiless god,
with scents, garlands, incenses, and food-offerings, the beautiful woman, / having then summoned a brāhmaṇa who knows dharma and has mastered the Veda,
one without physical defect, and having worshipped him with offerings of scent, flowers, and the like, / [should give] a prastha of rice grains along with a vessel of clarified butter
to that brāhmaṇa, saying, ‘May Mādhava be pleased!’ / When this most excellent twice-born has eaten food to his heart's content,
she should hold in her mind: ‘This is Kāmadeva for the purpose of pleasure.’ / Whatever the best of brāhmaṇas desires, that the charming woman should do;
and she, speaking with a smile, should surrender herself with all devotion. / In this way, on Sundays, she should perform all of this,
giving a prastha of rice grains until thirteen months have passed. / Then, when the thirteenth month has arrived, the fair lady,
discerning, should give to the brāhmaṇa an auspicious bed furnished with accessories, / with pillows, neatly arranged, with good bedding and a coverlet,
provided with a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, sandals, and a seat. / Having adorned him and his wife with gold threads and rings,
with fine garments, bracelets, incenses, garlands, and unguents, / [she should present] Kāmadeva together with his wife placed upon a jar of raw sugar,
set upon a copper vessel as a seat, covered with a golden-threaded cloth, / provided with a good bell-metal vessel and accompanied by a sugarcane stalk;
she should give it with this mantra, and likewise a milch cow: / ‘Just as I always see no difference between Kāma and Keśava,
so may the fulfillment of all my desires ever be granted, O brāhmaṇa!’ / And taking the golden deity, the best of the twice-born
should utter the Vedic mantra: ‘Who gave it? Kāma gave it.’ / Then, circumambulating and bidding farewell to the eminent twice-born,
she should take the bed, seat, and all the rest to the brāhmaṇa’s house. / From then on, whatever other man comes to her house for pleasure,
he should always be honored and worshipped on a Sunday. / In this way, every month up to the thirteenth, an excellent twice-born
having been gratified to his heart's desire, she should send him home; / and with his permission, until a handsome man comes to her.
If she herself encounters an obstacle from pregnancy, childbirth, or the king, / or whether it be divine, human, or caused by an eclipse,
she should offer fifty-eight turns according to her capacity. / This has indeed been fully explained, especially for you,
since this inherent duty of courtesans must always be observed in this world: / 'O God, just as you are never abandoned by your bed,
so, O Madhusūdana, may my bed also not be empty.' / She should cause the sound of singing and musical instruments to be made for the God of gods.
All this duty of courtesans has been told to you in its entirety, / which was formerly spoken by Puruhūta and by me among the Dānavīs.
All that applies right now to you as well; / it pacifies all sins and grants boundless reward.
This difficult vow has been spoken for auspicious women. / Whichever auspicious woman performs this entirely and fully, residing in the world of Mādhava,
worshipped by all the hosts of gods, she reaches the joy-giving abode of Viṣṇu. / Having explained this vow of giving love to women, that ascetic
said: 'They will all go to their own abode, and thus they will perform the vow, O god-born one!'

1.24.m: Brahmā said: / O Lord, tell me what grants boons to a man and a woman in this world, / by which grief, disease, fear, and sorrow do not arise.
Śaṃkara said: / On the second day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, Madhusūdana, / Keśava, always dwells in the ocean of milk accompanied by his wife.
Having worshipped Govinda on that day, one obtains all desires, / followed by [the merit of] gifts of cows, land, and gold for seven hundred aeons.
One should arrange the worship, beginning with the invocation, as before; / this second day is proclaimed by the name Aśūnyaśayanā.
On it, one should worship Viṣṇu according to rule with these mantras: / 'O bearer of the Śrīvatsa! O beloved of Śrī! O lord of Śrī! O Śrīdhara! O imperishable one!
May my household life, which grants dharma, wealth, and pleasure, not perish! / May the sacred fires and the deities not perish, O Puruṣottama!
May my ancestors not perish through a division between husband and wife! / Just as the divine Hari is never separated from Lakṣmī,
so, O God, may my bond with my wife never be broken! / O giver of boons, just as your couch is never empty of Lakṣmī,
so likewise, O Madhusūdana, may my bed not be empty!' / One should cause the sounds of singing and musical instruments to be made for the God of gods.
A bell may be used by one who is unable, since it embodies all musical instruments. / Having thus worshipped Govinda, one should eat food free of oil,
a meal at night without pungent or saline condiments, until four [months] are complete. / Then, when morning has come, along with the lord of Lakṣmī,
one should give an extraordinary bed supplied with lamps, food, and vessels, / accompanied by sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a chowrie, and a seat,
furnished with desired accessories, and covered with white flowers and garments, / to an unblemished brāhmaṇa, a Vaiṣṇava householder
who knows the Veda, and never to the husband of a barren woman. / Having seated the husband and wife there and decorated them according to rule,
one should give the wife a vessel filled with foods to be eaten and chewed; / and to the brāhmaṇa, a golden image of the God of gods
accompanied by its accessories, along with a water-pot, one should present. / Thus, whatever man performs the Aśūnyaśayana [vow] of Hari,
free from deceit regarding wealth and devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / he never suffers separation from his wife,
nor, O Brahmā, does a woman become a widow as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. / The couple never becomes deformed or afflicted with grief,
nor do sons, cattle, and jewels suffer ruin, O grandfather. / For seven thousand aeons and seven hundred aeons,
the one performing the Aśūnyaśayana [vow] is magnified in the world of Viṣṇu. / Brahmā said: / How does health, prosperity, an intellect rooted always in dharma,
freedom from defects, and supreme devotion to Viṣṇu arise? / Īśvara said: / Well asked, O Brahmā! I shall now tell you
[Hear] the dialogue of Virocana and the wise descendant of Bhṛgu. / Having seen the son of Prahlāda, sixteen years of age,
and this beauty of his, O Brahmā, that scion of Bhṛgu laughed: / 'Well done, well done, O mighty-armed Virocana! Blessings unto you!'
The slayer of gods asked him about that laughter of his: / 'O brāhmaṇa, for what reason was this laughter directed at me by you?
Why have you spoken thus to me, saying "Well done, well done"? Tell me!' / To him who spoke thus appropriately, the best of speakers replied:
'Out of wonder and because of the greatness of a vow, this laugh was made by me. / Formerly, for the destruction of Dakṣa, from the enraged wielder of the trident,
who had a terrifying face, a drop of sweat fell from his forehead; / splitting the seven subterranean realms, it burned the seven oceans.
He had many faces and eyes, terrible with blazing fire, / known as Vīrabhadra, endowed with myriad arms and feet.
Having crushed the sacrifice, there was again an inundation of beings; / from burning the three worlds, he was again restrained by Śiva:
"The destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice has been accomplished by you, O Vīrabhadra; / now enough with this deed of burning the world!
Because you bestow pacification, become the first among all the planets. / Joyful people of good lineage will perform worship of you who are self-restrained.
You will attain renown as Aṅgāraka, O son of the earth! / And you will have a second form in the heavenly realm.
And the people who worship you on the fourth day, / to them will belong boundless beauty, health, and prosperity."
Spoken to thus, that assumer of forms at will then attained tranquility; / he was born instantly, O king, and again attained planethood.
Once upon a time, you, standing by, saw his excellent worship, / guest-water and so on, being performed by a Śūdra.
Because of that, you were born handsome, a god who is a thunderbolt to the host of foes; / and since diverse, far-reaching splendor arose in you,
therefore the gods and Dānavas call you Virocana. / From your merely seeing that vow being performed by a Śūdra,
such an abundance of beauty [arose]—at this I was astonished. / Therefore it was said: 'Well done, well done!' Ah, supreme greatness!
Even for an onlooker, beauty arises; what then for the one who performs it? / And because with devotion you observed the giving of cows and so forth to the son of the earth with an uncritical mind,
therefore this birth of yours took place, O Daitya, in the womb of an enemy of the gods!' / Then, hearing that speech of the high-souled Bhārgava,
the heroic delight of Prahlāda questioned the descendant of Bhṛgu again. / Virocana said: / "O venerable one, I wish to hear that vow properly, according to reality."
and the gift being offered which was seen by me in another birth; / you ought to describe its greatness and procedure as they are.
Having heard his speech, the Brahmin spoke with respect: / "When the fourth lunar day falls on a Tuesday, O Dānava,
Then, adorned with rubies, he should take a bath using earth. / Having bathed, facing north, he should chant the mantra: 'Fire is the head of heaven …'.
A Śūdra, however, should remain silent, remembering Mars, devoid of sense pleasures. / Then, when the sun has set, he should smear with cow dung
the courtyard all around with flower garlands, unbroken rice, and water. / Having worshipped it, he should draw an eight-petaled lotus with saffron.
In the absence of saffron, red sandalwood is prescribed. / Four water-pots should be prepared, provided with snacks and foods,
filled with red rice grains and rubies. / Having placed them at the four corners, along with various fruits,
he should likewise arrange all perfumes, garlands, and other offerings. / Then, having worshipped a tawny cow with golden horns, silver hooves, a bronze milking pail, and draped in cloth,
a gentle bull with red hooves, capable of bearing a burden, and seven grains together with garments; / likewise, a thumb-sized human figure made of gold, with long rod-like arms,

four-armed, made of gold, placed upon molasses in a copper vessel filled with ghee; / [these] are to be given to a twice-born householder who knows the notes of the Sāmaveda, whose senses are conquered,

and who is endowed with [eloquent] speech, beauty, good conduct, and noble lineage, but not to one full of deceit. / 'O Son of the Earth, O highly fortunate one born from the sweat of the Wielder of the Pināka,
desiring beauty, I have surrendered to you; accept this guest-offering, homage be to you!' / Having offered the guest-offering with this mantra using water mixed with red sandalwood,
he should then worship the excellent twice-born with red garlands, garments, and other gifts. / With the very same mantra, he should give [the idol of] Mars together with a pair of cattle.
If able, he should also present a bed endowed with all furnishings. / Whatever is most cherished in the world, and whatever is beloved in his home,
all that should be given to a virtuous person by one desiring inexhaustible merit from the gift. / Then, having circumambulated and dismissed the best of the twice-born,
at night he should eat only milk; in this way [he should observe it] for eight Angāraka [Tuesdays], / or for four. The merit of that, I shall declare to you:
Endowed with beauty and good fortune in birth after birth, / devoted to Viṣṇu or to Śiva, that man becomes the ruler of the seven continents.
For seven thousand kalpas he is glorified in the world of Rudra. / Therefore, you too, O lord of Daityas, observe this vow!
Addressed thus by the descendant of Bhṛgu, the Daitya performed the entire vow. / You too, O king, perform all this, because the knowers of the Veda declare it to be imperishable."
And whoever hears this with undistracted mind, for him too the Lord provides everything.

1.25.m: Bhīṣma said: / 'For one incapable of fasting, yet desiring the same fruit / because of lack of practice or sickness, let the cherished vow be stated.'
Pulastya said: / 'For those incapable of fasting, eating at night is prescribed. / In which vow [this is done], hear that great vow here indeed.
It is called the Couch of the Sun (Ādityaśayana), where the worship of Śaṅkara is performed duly. / Under which conjunctions of asterisms the knowers of the Purāṇas declare [it]:
When Sunday falls on a seventh lunar day [conjoined] with the Hasta asterism, / and there is also a solar transit, that lunar day fulfills all desires.
One should worship the image of Umā and Maheśvara with the names of the Sun; / for one should worship both the image of the Sun and the Liṅga of Śiva,
since no difference is recognized anywhere between the Lord of Umā and the Sun. / Therefore, O best of kings, one should worship the Sun in the home.
Under Hasta, 'Homage to the Sun', the two feet [are worshipped]; and under Citrā, the ankles, to Arka; / under Svātī, the shanks, to Puruṣottama; and under Viśākhā, the knees, to the Creator (Dhātṛ);

likewise under Anurādhā, 'Homage to the Thousand-Rayed', the two thighs are to be worshipped; / under Jyeṣṭhā, 'Homage to the Bodiless', the private parts; and under Mūla, the hips, to Indra, the Fierce;
under the pair of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, the navel, 'Homage to Tvaṣṭṛ, Who Possesses Seven Horses'; / under Śravaṇa, the belly, to the Sharp-Rayed; under Dhaniṣṭhā, the back, to Vikartana;

under the asterism of the Lord of the Waters [Śatabhiṣak], the chest is to be worshipped, to the Destroyer of Darkness; / under the pair of Pūrvabhādrapadā and Uttarabhādrapadā, the two excellent arms are to be worshipped, to the Fierce-Rayed;
under Revatī, O king, the two hands are to be worshipped, to the Lord of Good Renown; / under Aśvinī, the nails are to be worshipped, 'Homage to the Bearer of the Burden of Seven Horses';

under Bharaṇī, the throat is to be worshipped, to the Harsh-Rayed Maker of Day; / under the asterism of Fire [Kṛttikā], the neck; and under Rohiṇī, O descendant of Bharata, the two lips are to be worshipped;

under Mṛgaśiras, the tongue of the Enemy of Tripura is to be worshipped; under Ārdrā, the teeth, 'Homage to you, O Hari!'; / and under Punarvasu, the nose of Śaṅkara is to be worshipped, 'Homage to Savitṛ!';

under Puṣya, the forehead, to the Beloved of the Lotus; the locks of hair, to the Bearer of the Body of the Vedas; / under Āśleṣā, the crown of the head, to the Beloved of the Gods; and under Maghā, the two ears are to be worshipped;
under Pūrvaphālgunī, the most venerable eyes of Śambhu, to the Delighter of Cows and Brahmins; / then under the asterism Uttaraphālgunī, the two eyebrows are to be worshipped, 'To the Lord of All!';

‘Homage to the Bearer of the noose, goad, lotus, trident, skull-cup, serpent, moon, and bow; / homage to Śiva, the root of destruction of Gayāsura, the Bodiless, the Triple City, Andhaka, and others!’

Having worshipped the limbs beginning with these, the head should be worshipped with [the mantra], "To the Lord of the Universe." / Here too, food without oil, meat, or alkali, and not the leftovers of another's meal, must be eaten.
Having thus observed nocturnal meals, O king, he should give under the Punarvasu [asterism] / a prastha of rice grains and clarified butter in a vessel of udumbara wood.
Placing it in a vessel, he should present it to a twice-born along with gold. / On the seventh [fast], a pair of garments should additionally be given at the conclusion.
When the fourteenth [fast] is reached, at the conclusion, O descendant of Bharata, / he should feed a Brahmin with devotion using jaggery, milk, ghee, and the like.
Having fashioned a golden eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, / pure, measuring eight finger-breadths, and provided with ruby petals,
and having prepared a couch of auspicious characteristics, devoid of inauspicious knots, / furnished with pillows and a canopy, having a fine mattress and coverings,
provided also with wooden shoes, leather shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, mirrors, / ornaments, fruits, garments, and ointments,
having placed that lotus upon it, and adorned [it], / he should give a tawny cow endowed with good qualities, draped in cloth, very gentle, giving milk,
with silver hooves, golden horns, together with her calf, and with a bronze milking pail; / he should give that cow with the mantra, not letting the forenoon pass:
‘Just as your solar couch is never vacant / in luster, patience, fortune, and prosperity, so may my prosperities be!’
‘Just as the gods know no supreme being other than you, O sinless one, / so deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence, which is full of endless sorrow!’
Then, having circumambulated, bowed down, and dismissed [the Brahmin], / he should convey the bed, cows, and all that to the home of the twice-born.

This vow of the Moon-Crested Lord should not be revealed to one of bad character, to a hypocrite, / nor to one who excessively reviles cows, Brahmins, gods, sages, and those engaged in improper deeds.

This secret, bliss-bestowing, and auspicious vow should be told to a devotee and one of restrained senses; / the knowers of the Veda declare that for men who have committed great sins, this brings the destruction of sin.
Separated neither from kin and sons nor from wealth and wives, gladdening the gods, / he never contracts disease, nor sorrow, nor delusion; likewise any woman who performs it with devotion.
In ancient times this was performed by Vasiṣṭha, Arjuna, Kubera, and Indra; / merely by reciting it, all sins go to destruction, there is no doubt in this.
He who recites or hears thus the repose of the Sun becomes beloved of Indra; / and whoever performs it here brings all his ancestors, even those who have gone to hell, to heaven.
The holy fig, the banyan, the cluster fig tree, / the nandīśa, the rose-apple tree, and the bael: [these] the great seers have proclaimed.
Starting with Mārgaśīrṣa, two months by two months in succession, / one should have the tooth-cleansing stick made from each one of these trees.
Upon its completion, one should give curd-rice, a canopy, banners, and a fly-whisk, / and to the twice-born water-jars furnished with the five gems.
One should not practice deceit regarding wealth; by practicing it, one would incur faults.
